t: LeetCode 1612 — Check If Two Expression Trees are Equivalent
o: Two binary expression trees built solely from the '+' operator are equivalent exactly when they evaluate to the same value for every possible assignment of the variables. Because addition is commutative and associative, neither tree shape nor operand order matters — only how many times each variable appears as a leaf. In Example 2, a + (b + c) and (b + c) + a both reduce to the multiset {a, b, c}, so the answer is true. In Example 3 the first tree yields {a, b, c} while the second yields {a, b, d}, so they differ. With up to 4999 nodes per tree, any linear (or even O(n log n)) comparison passes easily; the real task is recognizing that equivalence reduces to comparing character counts.
k: With only '+' as an operator, equivalence of two expression trees reduces to comparing the multisets of their leaf variables — structure is irrelevant.
A fixed 26-slot counter array turns the comparison into O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
Any traversal works: internal nodes are exactly the '+' nodes and operands are the leaves.

a.i: Traverse each tree, gathering the label of every leaf (any node whose value is not '+'). Sorting both collected lists and comparing them decides equivalence, because identical sorted multisets of operands guarantee identical sums regardless of association order.
s: DFS both trees, appending the character of every non-'+' node to a list.
Sort each list of operand characters.
Return true iff the two sorted lists are equal.
a.t: O(n log n) — visiting all n nodes plus sorting up to (n+1)/2 collected leaves.
a.sp: O(n) — storing the leaf characters of both trees.

a.i: Since operand labels are lowercase English letters, replace sorting with a 26-entry frequency array per tree. One traversal increments the counter of each leaf; comparing the two arrays element-wise is then sufficient and strictly faster than sorting.
s: DFS each tree; for every leaf increment counter[val - 'a'].
Return true iff the two arrays match in all 26 positions.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over each tree plus a constant-size comparison.
a.sp: O(h) recursion stack for height h; counters themselves are O(1).

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, jump straight to the counting solution — it shows you spotted the algebraic simplification immediately; mention the sort-based version only as a stepping stone. **Pitfalls:** wasting time comparing tree structures (shape genuinely does not matter here), and treating single-node trees incorrectly (a lone variable is equivalent only to the same variable).

**Follow-up ('-' operator):** subtraction destroys commutativity, so counts alone are insufficient. Propagate a signed coefficient per variable down the DFS (+1 along left branches, sign flipped when descending into the right child of a '-') and compare the resulting signed coefficient vectors. A randomized alternative — evaluate both trees under a few random assignments — gives a probabilistic answer useful for very deep trees.
